title: Which statements about powers are always, sometimes or never true?
description: Five statements about powers are each sorted as always true, only sometimes true or never true. One failing case breaks a claim of always, and regrouping the factors shows a statement holds for every number.
teaching_notes: One idea: one failing case breaks always, while regrouping the equal factors shows a statement holds for every number. Watch for students who test one number that works and decide the statement is always true.

video_script.why: The child can join powers by counting equal factors and now uses that counting to judge five statements about powers.
video_script.substitution: Five new statements about cubes, fourth powers, a fifth power, two cubes multiplied and a power of a prime, each judged by one test case or by regrouping.
video_script.anchor: five statement cards on the board, each placed in one of three trays after a test

final_answer.value: (i) Only sometimes true (ii) Always true (iii) Always true (iv) Always true (v) Never true
final_answer.spoken: statement one is only sometimes true; statements two, three and four are always true; and statement five is never true

never_show: statement one placed in the always true tray
maths_rules: (i) 8 = 2³ is a cube; 2² = 4 and 3² = 9, so 8 is not a square; 64 = 4³ = 8² is both; only sometimes true
(ii) n⁴ = n × n × n × n = (n × n) × (n × n) = (n²)²; always true
(iii) n⁵ = n³ × n², so n⁵ ÷ n³ = n²; always true
(iv) a³ × b³ = (a × a × a) × (b × b × b) = (a × b) × (a × b) × (a × b) = (a × b)³; always true
(v) a 4th power of a prime q has exponent a multiple of 4; 46 ÷ 4 = 11 remainder 2; also 46 ÷ 6 = 7 remainder 4; never true
video_script.design: One idea: a failing case breaks always, and regrouping proves it for every number. The five cards stay on the board all video; the verdict of the last card is left open until the answer; the check tries numbers on three statements.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about statements on powers.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Five statements are on the board.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is each one always true, only sometimes true, or never true?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one case that works and one that fails; regroup the equal factors

marks.fail: a tick and a cross appear for one case that works and one that fails
marks.regroup: equal factors are regrouped for every number

narration: <bookmark mark='fail'/>To test a statement, find one case that works and one that fails.
<bookmark mark='regroup'/>If we regroup the factors and the reason works for every number, the statement is always true.

beats.on_screen: Given: (i) cube numbers are also square numbers; (ii) fourth powers are also square numbers; (iii) the fifth power of a number is divisible by its cube; (iv) two cube numbers multiplied give a cube number; (v) q⁴⁶ is both a 4th power and a 6th power, q a prime number

marks.given: the first statement card is written
marks.prime: q is marked as a prime number

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, five statements about powers.
One, cube numbers are also square numbers.
Two, fourth powers are also square numbers.
<bookmark mark='s3'/>Three, the fifth power of a number is divisible by the cube of that number.
<bookmark mark='s4'/>Four, multiplying two cube numbers gives a cube number.
<bookmark mark='s5'/>Five, queue to the power forty six is both a fourth power and a sixth power.
<bookmark mark='prime'/>Here queue is a prime number.

beats.on_screen: To find: always true, only sometimes true or never true, for each statement
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to decide the verdict for each statement.

beats.on_screen: (i) 8 = 2³; 2² = 4, 3² = 9, so 8 is not a square; 64 = 4³ = 8²; (i) Only sometimes true

marks.one: the first statement card is lit up
marks.eight: 2³ = 8 is written with a cross beside square
marks.verdict: card (i) moves to the only sometimes tray

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step one, test cube numbers, the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='eight'/>Eight is two cubed.
It is not a square number, because two squared is four and three squared is nine.
<bookmark mark='sixtyfour'/>But sixty four is four cubed, and also eight squared.
<bookmark mark='verdict'/>Statement one is only sometimes true.

beats.on_screen: (ii) n⁴ = n × n × n × n = (n × n) × (n × n) = (n²)²; (ii) Always true

marks.two: n⁴ is written as four equal factors
marks.pairs: the four factors are grouped into two pairs
marks.verdict: card (ii) moves to the always tray

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, write a fourth power as four equal factors.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>Group the four factors into two pairs.
Each pair is the number squared, so the fourth power is that number squared, all squared.
<bookmark mark='verdict'/>Statement two is always true.

beats.on_screen: (iii) n⁵ = n³ × n²; n⁵ ÷ n³ = n²; (iii) Always true

marks.three: n⁵ is split as n³ × n²
marks.verdict: card (iii) moves to the always tray

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step three, the fifth power is the cube multiplied by the square.
<bookmark mark='divide'/>Dividing by the cube leaves the square.
<bookmark mark='verdict'/>Statement three is always true.

beats.on_screen: (iv) a³ × b³ = (a × a × a) × (b × b × b) = (a × b) × (a × b) × (a × b) = (a × b)³; (iv) Always true

marks.four: a³ and b³ are written as three a's and three b's
marks.pair: each a is paired with one b, three times
marks.verdict: card (iv) moves to the always tray

narration: <bookmark mark='four'/>Step four, take two cubes, eigh cubed and bee cubed.
Multiplied together, that is three eighs and three bees.
<bookmark mark='pair'/>Pair each eigh with one bee.
That is eigh times bee, three times, which is eigh times bee, all cubed.
<bookmark mark='verdict'/>Statement four is always true.

beats.on_screen: (v) a 4th power of a prime has an exponent that is a multiple of 4; 46 ÷ 4 = 11, 2 left over

marks.five: the rule for a 4th power of a prime is written
marks.left: the verdict of card (v) is left open

narration: <bookmark mark='five'/>Step five, a fourth power of a prime needs an exponent that is a multiple of four.
<bookmark mark='rem'/>Forty six divided by four is eleven, with two left over.
Forty six is not a multiple of four.
<bookmark mark='left'/>The verdict for statement five is left to find.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Step six, check with numbers.
Two cubed times three cubed is eight times twenty seven, which is two hundred sixteen.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Six cubed is also two hundred sixteen.
<bookmark mark='thirty'/>Two to the power five is thirty two, and thirty two divided by eight is four.
<bookmark mark='eightyone'/>Three to the power four is eighty one, which is nine squared.

beats.on_screen: Answer: (i) Only sometimes true; (ii) Always true; (iii) Always true; (iv) Always true; (v) Never true
narration: <bookmark mark='a1'/>Statement one is only sometimes true.
<bookmark mark='a2'/>Statements two, three and four are always true.
<bookmark mark='a3'/>Statement five is never true.
